title: The USA Road Trip Atlas & Planner: 50 Scenic Routes, Easy-to-Read Maps, and Must-See Stops
description: Some roads open only ten weeks a year, others run seventy miles between gas stations, and a few hang above the ocean for a day and a half of driving. America was built for the road trip, and this atlas maps fifty of the greatest, from the California cliffs to the harbors of Maine. Most road-trip books describe a handful of famous drives from behind a desk. This one plans all fifty, mile by mile, with a driver’s eye for what matters once you’re out there: when the passes open, where the fuel runs out, which stops earn the detour, and which rooms are gone if you wait. And the rules of the road trip have changed. The national parks raised the price of entry in 2026, added a surcharge for visitors from abroad, and now require timed-entry reservations at some of the most popular parks, while the historic lodges and small-town inns on the best routes book months ahead for the peak season. The best rooms, and the best timing, go to whoever planned first. Choose your drive by how much time you have or the season you can travel, then follow it from the first turn to the last, with every stop numbered on the map and described on the page beside it. Inside this book, you’ll find: 50 hand-picked scenic routes coast to coast, from Big Sur and the Pacific Coast Highway to the Blue Ridge Parkway, the Overseas Highway to Key West, Going-to-the-Sun Road, and the fall-color roads of New England 61 full-color, easy-to-read maps for every route and region Mile-by-mile directions for all fifty drives, with numbered must-see stops and why each one earns its place Know-before-you-go notes and an insider tip for every drive: seasonal closures, fuel gaps in empty country, crowds, and the best time of day to be there A “Find Your Trip” planner that sorts the drives by length and by season Desert

title: The National Road: Dispatches From a Changing America
description: This collection of "eloquent essays that examine the relationship between the American landscape and the national character" serves to remind us that despite our differences we all belong to the same land ( Publishers Weekly ). “How was it possible, I wondered, that all of this American land––in every direction––could be fastened together into a whole?” What does it mean when a nation accustomed to moving begins to settle down, when political discord threatens unity, and when technology disrupts traditional ways of building communities? Is a shared soil enough to reinvigorate a national spirit? From the embaattled newsrooms of small town newspapers to the pornography film sets of the Los Angeles basin, from the check–out lanes of Dollar General to the holy sites of Mormonism, from the nation’s highest peaks to the razed remains of a cherished home, like a latter–day Woody Guthrie, Tom Zoellner takes to the highways and byways of a vast land in search of the soul of its people.
